title: Calculus III (Multivariable)
description: Calculus III extends calculus to functions, curves, surfaces, and fields in two, three, and higher dimensions. This unified course gives all twelve programs the same rigorous mathematical core while rotating applications through mechanics, electromagnetism, transport, thermodynamics, optimization, probability, economics, and quantitative modeling. Students work geometrically, symbolically, numerically, and computationally, and they must communicate assumptions, orientation, units, and theorem hypotheses.

topics.title: Vectors, Matrices, and Geometry in Space
topics.description: Multivariable calculus begins with a language for position, direction, geometry, and linear change. Vectors describe quantities with magnitude and direction, while elementary matrix notation prepares students to express systems, transformations, and derivatives compactly.

children.title: Coordinate systems and geometry in two and three dimensions
children.description: A reliable spatial picture is essential for setting domains, interpreting level sets, and choosing coordinates that fit a problem's symmetry.

children.title: Cartesian coordinates, distance, midpoint, spheres, cylinders, and traces
Cylindrical and spherical coordinates as geometric descriptions
Quadratic surfaces: ellipsoids, paraboloids, hyperboloids, and cones
Sketching surfaces from equations, cross-sections, symmetry, and intercepts
Vector algebra and geometric products
children.description: Vector operations convert geometric questions about angles, projections, areas, orientation, force, and torque into calculations.

children.title: Components, magnitude, unit vectors, addition, and scalar multiplication
Dot product, angles, orthogonality, projection, and work
Cross product, orientation, area, torque, and the scalar triple product
Vector identities and proof-aware geometric reasoning
Lines, planes, matrices, and linear systems
children.description: Parametric descriptions and small matrix systems connect spatial geometry to the derivative-matrix viewpoint used later in the course.

children.title: Vector and parametric equations of lines
Normal-vector equations of planes and distances to planes
Intersections, parallelism, skew lines, and geometric constraints
Matrix notation, linear maps, determinants, and solving small systems

topics.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion
topics.description: Vector-valued functions describe curves and trajectories in space. Their derivatives separate motion into velocity, acceleration, speed, direction, and curvature, creating a bridge from single-variable calculus to mechanics and field-based models.

children.title: Curves and vector-valued functions
children.description: A parameter lets all coordinates vary together, representing paths that may loop, intersect, or move through three dimensions.

children.title: Parametric curves, orientation, domains, and traces
Limits, continuity, derivatives, and integrals component by component
Tangent lines and smoothness of a parametrized curve
Reparameterization and the role of the parameter
Position, velocity, acceleration, and speed
children.description: Derivatives of a position vector give a complete kinematic description and make units and reference frames explicit.

children.title: Position, displacement, velocity, speed, and acceleration
Projectile and orbital-style motion under simplified force laws
Recovering position from velocity or acceleration and initial data
Interpreting vector components, signs, and units
Arc length, curvature, and moving frames
children.description: Arc length measures distance along a curve, while curvature and moving unit vectors describe how sharply and in what direction a trajectory turns.

children.title: Arc length and the arc-length parameter
Unit tangent vector and curvature
Principal normal and tangential-normal acceleration components
Optional enrichment: binormal vector, torsion, and Frenet frame

topics.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity
topics.description: Functions of several variables model quantities influenced by multiple inputs. This unit develops their geometry and the path-independent limiting behavior required before derivatives and approximations can be trusted.

children.title: Domains, graphs, and level sets
children.description: Different representations reveal different features: a graph shows height, a level set shows where output is constant, and a domain records which inputs are meaningful.

children.title: Functions from R^n to R and from R^n to R^m
Domains, ranges, graphs, level curves, level surfaces, and contour maps
Sections, traces, and data-based visualizations
Applications to temperature, concentration, cost, utility, and energy landscapes
Multivariable limits
children.description: A multivariable limit must be the same along every possible approach, so checking a few paths can disprove a limit but usually cannot prove one.

children.title: Neighborhoods, distance, and approaching a point in multiple dimensions
Limits by substitution and algebraic simplification
Path tests for nonexistence
Bounding, squeeze arguments, and polar-coordinate estimates for existence
Continuity and local behavior
children.description: Continuity ensures that nearby inputs produce nearby outputs and supports composition, extreme-value arguments, integration, and numerical modeling.

children.title: Continuity at a point and on a region
Continuity of sums, products, quotients, and compositions
Boundary behavior and discontinuity classification
Closed and bounded regions, intuitive compactness and existence of extrema

topics.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentiability, and the Chain Rule
topics.description: Partial derivatives measure one-input-at-a-time change, but differentiability is the stronger claim that one linear map approximates all small changes at once. This distinction is central to reliable modeling, optimization, and computation.

children.title: Partial and higher-order derivatives
children.description: Holding other inputs fixed isolates sensitivity to one variable and produces the building blocks for gradients, Hessians, and differential equations.

children.title: First partial derivatives from formulas, tables, and limits
Units and ceteris-paribus interpretation
Second and mixed partial derivatives
Clairaut's theorem and the conditions for equality of mixed partials
Differentiability, tangent planes, and total differentials
children.description: Differentiability means the function has a best local linear approximation, not merely that its partial derivatives exist.

children.title: Tangent planes and linearization
Total differentials and propagated measurement error
Sufficient conditions for differentiability and counterexamples
Derivative matrices and the Jacobian as a linear map
Multivariable chain rules and implicit differentiation
children.description: The chain rule tracks how change propagates through a dependency network and provides the derivative of a composition of multivariable maps.

children.title: Chain rule along a parametrized path
Tree diagrams and dependency graphs
Matrix form of the chain rule for R^n to R^m maps
Implicit differentiation and sensitivity in constrained relationships

topics.title: Gradient, Directional Derivatives, and Local Approximation
topics.description: The gradient packages all first-order information for a scalar field. It points in the direction of steepest increase, stands perpendicular to level sets, and drives approximation, optimization, flux, and field models.

children.title: Directional derivatives and the gradient
children.description: A directional derivative asks how a scalar field changes along a chosen unit direction. The gradient answers all such questions through one dot product.

children.title: Directional derivative from a path and from the gradient formula
Unit-direction requirement and normalization
Maximum rate of change and steepest ascent or descent
Gradient orthogonality to level curves and level surfaces
Tangent objects and normal vectors
children.description: Gradients supply normal vectors to implicit curves and surfaces, making tangent lines and tangent planes systematic.

children.title: Tangent lines to level curves
Tangent planes and normal lines to level surfaces
Angle of intersection and orthogonality
Applications to terrain, thermodynamics, fields, and implicit geometry
First- and second-order Taylor approximation
children.description: Taylor approximation extends tangent-plane reasoning by using gradient and curvature information to predict nearby values and assess local error.

children.title: First-order approximation and differentials
Jacobian-based approximation for vector-valued maps
Hessian matrix and quadratic terms
Error, scaling, sensitivity, and the limits of local models

topics.title: Unconstrained and Constrained Optimization
topics.description: Optimization identifies best feasible choices in design, economics, science, and operations. A world-class treatment combines geometric intuition, derivative tests, boundary analysis, and careful interpretation rather than relying on formulas alone.

children.title: Critical points and local classification
children.description: At an interior differentiable optimum the gradient vanishes, but a critical point may be a maximum, minimum, saddle, or inconclusive case.

children.title: Critical points and stationary conditions
Hessian matrix and the two-variable second-derivative test
Positive and negative definiteness as enrichment
Saddle points, degeneracy, and inconclusive tests
Global extrema and boundary analysis
children.description: Global optimization requires a complete search over the interior and boundary of the feasible region, supported by an existence theorem when appropriate.

children.title: Extreme Value Theorem on closed, bounded regions
Boundary parameterization and endpoint checks
Piecewise or non-smooth feasible boundaries
Comparing all candidates and interpreting feasibility
Lagrange multipliers and applications
children.description: At a smooth constrained optimum, objective and constraint gradients align. The multiplier can also carry a useful marginal or sensitivity meaning.

children.title: One equality constraint and the gradient-parallel condition
Solving the multiplier system and checking candidates
Multiple constraints and constraint qualification as enrichment
Engineering design, economic allocation, chemistry, and least-squares examples

topics.title: Double Integrals and Integration over Planar Regions
topics.description: Double integrals accumulate density, probability, cost, mass, or another local quantity across a two-dimensional region. The main intellectual work is describing the region and choosing an efficient order or coordinate system.

children.title: Riemann sums and iterated integrals
children.description: A double integral is the limit of weighted sums over small area elements. Fubini's theorem converts many such limits into repeated one-variable integrals.

children.title: Double Riemann sums and signed volume
Fubini's theorem and iterated integrals on rectangles

Numerical approximation from grids or sampled data
General regions and changing order

children.title: Vertically and horizontally simple regions
Sketching bounds before integrating
Changing the order of integration
Splitting non-simple regions into valid pieces
Polar coordinates and planar applications

children.title: Cartesian-polar conversion and polar regions
Area element dA = r dr dtheta
Mass, moments, center of mass, and probability density
Radially symmetric models and normalization checks

topics.title: Triple Integrals, Coordinate Systems, and Change of Variables
topics.description: Triple integrals extend accumulation to volumes, while a general change of variables adapts the coordinate grid to the geometry. The Jacobian determinant measures the local scaling of area or volume under that transformation.

children.title: Triple integrals in rectangular coordinates
children.description: A three-dimensional region can be sliced and projected in several ways. A clear sketch and consistent bounds are essential.

children.title: Iterated triple integrals and order of integration

General transformations and Jacobians

topics.title: Vector Fields, Line Integrals, and Conservative Fields
topics.description: Vector fields assign a vector to each point, representing velocity, force, electrical influence, gradients, or transport. Line integrals measure accumulated work, circulation, or scalar density along a curve.

topics.title: Green's Theorem in the Plane
topics.description: Green's theorem equates circulation or flux around a closed planar boundary with a double integral over the enclosed region. It is the first major example of a boundary-interior principle that unifies vector calculus.

children.title: Circulation form
children.description: The circulation form converts a positively oriented boundary integral into the accumulated scalar curl over the region.

Connections between circulation and flux forms

topics.title: Parametric Surfaces and Surface Integrals
